To express the standard basis vectors as linear combinations of $\alpha _1, \alpha _2, \alpha _3$, we solve the systems \begin{align*} (1, 0, 0) &= a_{11} \alpha _1 + a_{12} \alpha _2 + a_{13} \alpha _3, \\ (0, 1, 0) &= a_{21} \alpha _1 + a_{22} \alpha _2 + a_{23} \alpha _3, \\ (0, 0, 1) &= a_{31} \alpha _1 + a_{32} \alpha _2 + a_{33} \alpha _3. \end{align*} Equivalently, we can row-reduce the augmented matrix \begin{align*} \quad & \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 1 & 0 & -1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right] \\ \xrightarrow{R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - R_1} & \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 1 & 0 & -1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right] \\ \xrightarrow{R_2 \leftrightarrow \frac{R_2}{2}} & \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 1 & 0 & -1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -\nicefrac{1}{2} & \nicefrac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 2 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right] \\ \xrightarrow{R_3 \rightarrow R_3 + 3R_2} & \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 1 & 0 & -1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -\nicefrac{1}{2} & \nicefrac{1}{2} & 0 \\[1ex] 0 & 0 & 5 & -\nicefrac{3}{2} & \nicefrac{3}{2} & 1 \end{array} \right] \\ \xrightarrow{R_3 \rightarrow \frac{R_3}{5}} & \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 1 & 0 & -1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -\nicefrac{1}{2} & \nicefrac{1}{2} & 0 \\[1ex] 0 & 0 & 1 & -\nicefrac{3}{10} & \nicefrac{3}{10} & \nicefrac{1}{5} \end{array} \right] \\ \xrightarrow[R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - R_3]{R_1 \rightarrow R_1 + R_3}& \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 & \nicefrac{7}{10} & \nicefrac{3}{10} & \nicefrac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -\nicefrac{1}{5} & \nicefrac{1}{5} & -\nicefrac{1}{5} \\[1ex] 0 & 0 & 1 & -\nicefrac{3}{10} & \nicefrac{3}{10} & \nicefrac{1}{5} \end{array} \right]. \end{align*}
Therefore, we have \begin{align*} (1, 0, 0) &= \frac{7}{10} \alpha _1 + \frac{3}{10} \alpha _2 + \frac{1}{5} \alpha _3, \\ (0, 1, 0) &= -\frac{1}{5} \alpha _1 + \frac{1}{5} \alpha _2 - \frac{1}{5} \alpha _3, \\[1ex] (0, 0, 1) &= -\frac{3}{10} \alpha _1 + \frac{3}{10} \alpha _2 + \frac{1}{5} \alpha _3. \end{align*}

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - Three linearly dependent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$, any two of which are linearly independent
problems.problem: Find three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ which are linearly dependent, and are such that any two of them are linearly independent.
problems.hint: • Two vectors are linearly dependent exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other. Try two vectors that are not multiples of each other, together with their sum.
problems.solution:
Take \[ \alpha _1 = (1, 0, 0), \quad \alpha _2 = (0, 1, 0), \quad \alpha _3 = (1, 1, 0). \] These are linearly dependent, since \[ 1 \cdot \alpha _1 + 1 \cdot \alpha _2 + (-1) \cdot \alpha _3 = (0,0,0) \] is a linear relation in which not all coefficients are zero.
Now we check the pairs. Two vectors are linearly dependent if and only if one of them is a scalar multiple of the other (see Exercise 2.3.1).
  1. $\alpha _1, \alpha _2$: if $\alpha _1 = c\, \alpha _2$, then comparing first coordinates gives $1 = 0$, which is impossible; similarly $\alpha _2 = c\, \alpha _1$ is impossible.
  2. $\alpha _1, \alpha _3$: if $\alpha _3 = c\, \alpha _1 = (c, 0, 0)$, the second coordinate gives $1 = 0$; if $\alpha _1 = c\, \alpha _3 = (c, c, 0)$, the first coordinate gives $c = 1$ and then the second gives $0 = 1$.
  3. $\alpha _2, \alpha _3$: the same argument with the roles of the first two coordinates exchanged.
Hence any two of $\alpha _1, \alpha _2, \alpha _3$ are linearly independent, while all three together are linearly dependent.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - The space of $2 \times 2$ matrices has dimension $4$
problems.problem: Let $V$ be the vector space of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over the field $F$. Prove that $V$ has dimension $4$ by exhibiting a basis for $V$ which has four elements.
problems.hint: • Consider the matrices which have a single entry equal to $1$ and all other entries equal to $0$.
problems.solution:
Let \[ E_{11} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad E_{12} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad E_{21} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad E_{22} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \] We show that $\{ E_{11}, E_{12}, E_{21}, E_{22} \}$ is a basis of $V$.
Spanning. For any $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \in V$ we have \[ A = a E_{11} + b E_{12} + c E_{21} + d E_{22}. \]
Linear independence. If $x_1 E_{11} + x_2 E_{12} + x_3 E_{21} + x_4 E_{22} = 0$, then \[ \begin{bmatrix} x_1 & x_2 \\ x_3 & x_4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \] so $x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = x_4 = 0$.
Therefore these four matrices form a basis of $V$, and $\dim V = 4$.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - Dimensions of $W_1$, $W_2$, $W_1 + W_2$ and $W_1 \cap W_2$ in the space of $2 \times 2$ matrices
problems.problem:
Let $V$ be the vector space of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over the field $F$. Let $W_1$ be the set of matrices of the form \[ \begin{bmatrix} x & -x \\ y & z \end{bmatrix} \] and let $W_2$ be the set of matrices of the form \[ \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ -a & c \end{bmatrix}. \]
  1. Prove that $W_1$ and $W_2$ are subspaces of $V$.
  2. Find the dimensions of $W_1$, $W_2$, $W_1 + W_2$ and $W_1 \cap W_2$.
problems.hint:
• Write a general element of $W_1$ as $x A_1 + y A_2 + z A_3$ for three fixed matrices; do the same for $W_2$.
  • For the dimension of the sum use $\dim (W_1 + W_2) = \dim W_1 + \dim W_2 - \dim (W_1 \cap W_2)$.
problems.solution:
(a) Every element of $W_1$ can be written as \[ \begin{bmatrix} x & -x \\ y & z \end{bmatrix} = x \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + y \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + z \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \] and conversely every such linear combination is in $W_1$. So $W_1$ is the span of three matrices, hence a subspace of $V$. In the same way \[ \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ -a & c \end{bmatrix} = a \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + b \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + c \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \] so $W_2$ is a subspace of $V$.
(b) The three matrices spanning $W_1$ are linearly independent: if the combination above is the zero matrix then the $(1,1)$, $(2,1)$ and $(2,2)$ entries give $x = y = z = 0$. Hence $\dim W_1 = 3$. Similarly, the $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$ and $(2,2)$ entries show that the three matrices spanning $W_2$ are independent, so $\dim W_2 = 3$.
A matrix $\begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix}$ lies in $W_1$ if and only if $q = -p$, and lies in $W_2$ if and only if $r = -p$. Hence \[ W_1 \cap W_2 = \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} x & -x \\ -x & z \end{bmatrix} : x, z \in F \right\} = \operatorname{span} \left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \right\}, \] and these two matrices are clearly independent. So $\dim (W_1 \cap W_2) = 2$.
Finally, \[ \dim (W_1 + W_2) = \dim W_1 + \dim W_2 - \dim (W_1 \cap W_2) = 3 + 3 - 2 = 4. \] Since $\dim V = 4$ (Exercise 2.3.6), we get $W_1 + W_2 = V$.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - A basis of $2 \times 2$ matrices consisting of idempotents
problems.problem: Let $V$ be the space of $2 \times 2$ matrices over the field $F$. Find a basis $\{ A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4 \}$ for $V$ such that $A_j^2 = A_j$ for each $j$.
problems.hint: • $E_{11}$ and $E_{22}$ are idempotent. Look for two more idempotent matrices with a $1$ in the $(1,1)$ position.
problems.solution:
Take \[ A_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad A_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad A_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad A_4 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]
Each $A_j$ is idempotent. Clearly $A_1^2 = A_1$ and $A_2^2 = A_2$. Also \[ A_3^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = A_3, \qquad A_4^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = A_4. \]
They form a basis. Suppose $a A_1 + b A_2 + c A_3 + d A_4 = 0$. Then \[ \begin{bmatrix} a + c + d & c \\ d & b \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \] which gives $c = 0$, $d = 0$, $b = 0$ and then $a = 0$. So the four matrices are linearly independent. Since $\dim V = 4$ (Exercise 2.3.6), four linearly independent vectors form a basis of $V$.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - If $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are linearly independent, so are $\alpha + \beta$, $\beta + \gamma$, $\gamma + \alpha$
problems.problem: Let $V$ be a vector space over a subfield $F$ of the complex numbers. Suppose $\alpha$, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ are linearly independent vectors in $V$. Prove that $(\alpha + \beta)$, $(\beta + \gamma)$ and $(\gamma + \alpha)$ are linearly independent.
problems.hint: • Start from $a(\alpha + \beta) + b(\beta + \gamma) + c(\gamma + \alpha) = 0$, collect the coefficients of $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$, and use that $2 \neq 0$ in $F$.
problems.solution:
Suppose $a, b, c \in F$ satisfy \[ a(\alpha + \beta) + b(\beta + \gamma) + c(\gamma + \alpha) = 0. \] Rearranging, \[ (a + c)\, \alpha + (a + b)\, \beta + (b + c)\, \gamma = 0. \] Since $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are linearly independent, \[ a + c = 0, \qquad a + b = 0, \qquad b + c = 0. \]
Adding the three equations gives $2(a + b + c) = 0$. Since $F$ is a subfield of $\mathbb{C}$, $2 \neq 0$ in $F$, so $a + b + c = 0$. Subtracting each of the three equations from this one gives $b = 0$, $c = 0$ and $a = 0$. Hence $\alpha + \beta$, $\beta + \gamma$, $\gamma + \alpha$ are linearly independent.
Remark. The only place where we used that $F \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is $2 \neq 0$. Over a field in which $1 + 1 = 0$ the statement fails; see Exercise 2.3.13.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - A vector space spanned by finitely many vectors is finite-dimensional
problems.problem: Let $V$ be a vector space over the field $F$. Suppose there are a finite number of vectors $\alpha _1, \dots, \alpha _r$ in $V$ which span $V$. Prove that $V$ is finite-dimensional.
problems.hint: • Among the subsets of $\{ \alpha _1, \dots, \alpha _r \}$ which are linearly independent, choose one with the largest number of elements. Show that it spans $V$.
problems.solution:
If $V = \{ 0 \}$ there is nothing to prove (the empty set is a basis), so assume $V \neq \{ 0 \}$. Let $S = \{ \alpha _1, \dots, \alpha _r \}$. The subsets of $S$ that are linearly independent form a finite, nonempty family (any single non-zero $\alpha _i$ is such a subset). Choose one, say $B$, with the largest possible number of elements.
We claim that every $\alpha _i$ is a linear combination of the vectors in $B$. This is clear if $\alpha _i \in B$. If $\alpha _i \notin B$, then $B \cup \{ \alpha _i \}$ has more elements than $B$, so by the choice of $B$ it is linearly dependent: there is a relation \[ c\, \alpha _i + \sum_{\beta \in B} c_\beta\, \beta = 0 \] with not all coefficients zero. Here $c \neq 0$, since otherwise this would be a non-trivial relation among the vectors of $B$. Dividing by $c$ expresses $\alpha _i$ as a linear combination of the vectors in $B$.
Hence $\operatorname{span} B$ contains every $\alpha _i$, and therefore contains $\operatorname{span} S = V$. So $B$ is a linearly independent set that spans $V$, that is, a basis of $V$ with at most $r$ elements. Therefore $V$ is finite-dimensional and $\dim V \leq r$.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - Trace-zero complex $2 \times 2$ matrices as a real vector space
problems.problem:
Let $V$ be the set of all $2 \times 2$ matrices $A$ with complex entries which satisfy $A_{11} + A_{22} = 0$.
  1. Show that $V$ is a vector space over the field of real numbers, with the usual operations of matrix addition and multiplication of a matrix by a scalar.
  2. Find a basis for this vector space.
  3. Let $W$ be the set of all matrices $A$ in $V$ such that $A_{21} = - \overline{A_{12}}$ (the bar denotes complex conjugation). Prove that $W$ is a subspace of $V$ and find a basis for $W$.
problems.hint:
• Each complex entry contributes two real parameters, its real and imaginary parts.
  • For (c), note that complex conjugation is additive and commutes with multiplication by real numbers (but not by complex numbers).
problems.solution:
(a) The set $M$ of all complex $2 \times 2$ matrices is a vector space over $\mathbb{C}$, hence also over $\mathbb{R}$ (restrict the scalars). So it is enough to show that $V$ is a subspace of $M$ over $\mathbb{R}$. The zero matrix is in $V$. If $A, B \in V$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, then \[ (cA + B)_{11} + (cA + B)_{22} = c (A_{11} + A_{22}) + (B_{11} + B_{22}) = 0, \] so $cA + B \in V$.
(b) A matrix in $V$ has the form \[ A = \begin{bmatrix} a_1 + \iota a_2 & b_1 + \iota b_2 \\ c_1 + \iota c_2 & -a_1 - \iota a_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad a_k, b_k, c_k \in \mathbb{R}. \] Hence $A = a_1 M_1 + a_2 M_2 + b_1 M_3 + b_2 M_4 + c_1 M_5 + c_2 M_6$, where \[ M_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \; M_2 = \begin{bmatrix} \iota & 0 \\ 0 & -\iota \end{bmatrix}, \; M_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \; M_4 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \iota \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \; M_5 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \; M_6 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ \iota & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \] These six matrices span $V$ over $\mathbb{R}$. They are also independent over $\mathbb{R}$: if the real combination above is the zero matrix, then its entries $a_1 + \iota a_2$, $b_1 + \iota b_2$, $c_1 + \iota c_2$ vanish, so all six real coefficients are $0$. Thus $\{ M_1, \dots, M_6 \}$ is a basis and $\dim_{\mathbb{R}} V = 6$.
(c) The zero matrix is in $W$. If $A, B \in W$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, then, since $\overline{c} = c$, \[ (cA + B)_{21} = c A_{21} + B_{21} = -c\, \overline{A_{12}} - \overline{B_{12}} = -\overline{c A_{12} + B_{12}} = -\overline{(cA + B)_{12}}, \] so $cA + B \in W$ and $W$ is a subspace of $V$. (It is not closed under multiplication by $\iota$, which is why we regard $V$ as a real vector space.)
With the notation of (b), the condition $A_{21} = -\overline{A_{12}}$ reads $c_1 + \iota c_2 = -b_1 + \iota b_2$, i.e. $c_1 = -b_1$ and $c_2 = b_2$. Hence the elements of $W$ are exactly \[ \begin{bmatrix} a_1 + \iota a_2 & b_1 + \iota b_2 \\ -b_1 + \iota b_2 & -a_1 - \iota a_2 \end{bmatrix} = a_1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} + a_2 \begin{bmatrix} \iota & 0 \\ 0 & -\iota \end{bmatrix} + b_1 \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + b_2 \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \iota \\ \iota & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \] As in (b), these four matrices are linearly independent over $\mathbb{R}$, so they form a basis of $W$ and $\dim_{\mathbb{R}} W = 4$.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - The space of $m \times n$ matrices has dimension $mn$
problems.problem: Prove that the space of all $m \times n$ matrices over the field $F$ has dimension $mn$, by exhibiting a basis for this space.
problems.hint: • Generalise Exercise 2.3.6: use the matrices with exactly one entry equal to $1$.
problems.solution:
For $1 \leq p \leq m$ and $1 \leq q \leq n$ let $E^{pq}$ be the $m \times n$ matrix whose $(p,q)$ entry is $1$ and all of whose other entries are $0$; in symbols, $(E^{pq})_{ij} = \delta_{ip}\, \delta_{jq}$. There are $mn$ such matrices.
Spanning. If $A = (A_{ij})$ is any $m \times n$ matrix, then \[ A = \sum_{p=1}^{m} \sum_{q=1}^{n} A_{pq}\, E^{pq}, \] because the $(i,j)$ entry of the right-hand side is $\sum_{p,q} A_{pq}\, \delta_{ip} \delta_{jq} = A_{ij}$.
Linear independence. If $\sum_{p,q} c_{pq} E^{pq} = 0$, then by the same computation the $(i,j)$ entry of the left-hand side is $c_{ij}$, so every $c_{ij} = 0$.
Hence $\{ E^{pq} : 1 \leq p \leq m, \ 1 \leq q \leq n \}$ is a basis, and the space of $m \times n$ matrices over $F$ has dimension $mn$.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - Exercise 2.3.9 over the field with two elements
problems.problem: Discuss Exercise 2.3.9 when $V$ is a vector space over the field with two elements, $F = \{ 0, 1 \}$ with $1 + 1 = 0$. That is: if $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are linearly independent vectors in $V$, are $\alpha + \beta$, $\beta + \gamma$, $\gamma + \alpha$ linearly independent?
problems.hint: • Add the three vectors $\alpha + \beta$, $\beta + \gamma$, $\gamma + \alpha$.
problems.solution:
The answer is no: over the field with two elements the three vectors are always linearly dependent. Indeed, \[ 1 \cdot (\alpha + \beta) + 1 \cdot (\beta + \gamma) + 1 \cdot (\gamma + \alpha) = (1 + 1)(\alpha + \beta + \gamma) = 0 \cdot (\alpha + \beta + \gamma) = 0, \] and the coefficients $1, 1, 1$ are not all zero.
For a concrete example, take $V = F^3$ and $\alpha = (1,0,0)$, $\beta = (0,1,0)$, $\gamma = (0,0,1)$, which are linearly independent. Then \[ \alpha + \beta = (1,1,0), \quad \beta + \gamma = (0,1,1), \quad \gamma + \alpha = (1,0,1), \] and $(1,1,0) + (0,1,1) + (1,0,1) = (2,2,2) = (0,0,0)$ in $F^3$.
This shows exactly where the proof of Exercise 2.3.9 breaks down: there we concluded $a + b + c = 0$ from $2(a + b + c) = 0$, which requires $2 \neq 0$ in the field.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - $\mathbb{R}$ is not finite-dimensional over $\mathbb{Q}$
problems.problem: Let $V$ be the set of real numbers. Regard $V$ as a vector space over the field of rational numbers, with the usual operations. Prove that this vector space is not finite-dimensional.
problems.hint: • If $\{ \beta _1, \dots, \beta _n \}$ were a basis, every real number would be determined by an $n$-tuple of rational numbers. Compare cardinalities.
problems.solution:
Suppose, to the contrary, that $V = \mathbb{R}$ has a finite basis $\{ \beta _1, \dots, \beta _n \}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Then every real number $x$ can be written uniquely as \[ x = q_1 \beta _1 + q_2 \beta _2 + \dots + q_n \beta _n, \qquad q_i \in \mathbb{Q}. \] So the map \[ \mathbb{Q}^n \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad (q_1, \dots, q_n) \mapsto q_1 \beta _1 + \dots + q_n \beta _n \] is a bijection (onto because the $\beta _i$ span, one-to-one because they are independent).
But $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable, hence so is the finite product $\mathbb{Q}^n$, while $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable. A countable set cannot be in bijection with an uncountable one. This contradiction shows that $\mathbb{R}$ has no finite basis over $\mathbb{Q}$, i.e., it is not finite-dimensional. (The case $n = 0$ is also excluded, since $\mathbb{R} \neq \{ 0 \}$.)

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - Coordinates of the standard basis vectors in a basis of $\mathbb{R}^4$
problems.problem:
Show that the vectors
    \[
        \alpha _1 = (1, 1, 0, 0), \quad \alpha _2 = (0, 0, 1, 1), \quad \alpha _3 = (1, 0, 0, 4), \quad \alpha _4 = (0, 0, 0, 2)
    \]
    form a basis for $\mathbb{R}^4$. Find the coordinates of each of the standard basis vectors in the ordered basis $\{ \alpha _1, \alpha _2, \alpha _3, \alpha _4 \}$.
problems.hint: • Solve $x_1 \alpha _1 + x_2 \alpha _2 + x_3 \alpha _3 + x_4 \alpha _4 = (a, b, c, d)$ for arbitrary $a, b, c, d$. If the solution always exists and is unique, the vectors form a basis.
problems.solution:
We have \[ x_1 \alpha _1 + x_2 \alpha _2 + x_3 \alpha _3 + x_4 \alpha _4 = (x_1 + x_3,\ x_1,\ x_2,\ x_2 + 4x_3 + 2x_4). \] Setting this equal to $(a, b, c, d)$ gives $x_1 = b$, $x_2 = c$, $x_3 = a - b$ and $x_4 = \frac{1}{2}\big( d - c - 4(a - b) \big)$. So for every $(a,b,c,d) \in \mathbb{R}^4$ there is exactly one solution. Existence means that $\alpha _1, \dots, \alpha _4$ span $\mathbb{R}^4$, and uniqueness (for $(a,b,c,d) = 0$) means that they are linearly independent. Hence they form a basis.
Using these formulas:
  1. $\epsilon _1 = (1,0,0,0)$: coordinates $(0, 0, 1, -2)$, i.e. $\epsilon _1 = \alpha _3 - 2\alpha _4$.
  2. $\epsilon _2 = (0,1,0,0)$: coordinates $(1, 0, -1, 2)$, i.e. $\epsilon _2 = \alpha _1 - \alpha _3 + 2\alpha _4$.
  3. $\epsilon _3 = (0,0,1,0)$: coordinates $\left(0, 1, 0, -\frac{1}{2}\right)$, i.e. $\epsilon _3 = \alpha _2 - \frac{1}{2}\alpha _4$.
  4. $\epsilon _4 = (0,0,0,1)$: coordinates $\left(0, 0, 0, \frac{1}{2}\right)$, i.e. $\epsilon _4 = \frac{1}{2}\alpha _4$.
One can check each directly; for example $\alpha _1 - \alpha _3 + 2\alpha _4 = (1,1,0,0) - (1,0,0,4) + (0,0,0,4) = (0,1,0,0)$.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - Coordinates of $(1,0,1)$ in a basis of $\mathbb{C}^3$
problems.problem:
Find the coordinate matrix of the vector $(1, 0, 1)$ in the basis of $\mathbb{C}^3$ consisting of the vectors
    \[
        (2\iota, 1, 0), \quad (2, -1, 1), \quad (0, 1 + \iota, 1 - \iota),
    \]
    in that order.
problems.hint: • Write $(1,0,1) = x(2\iota, 1, 0) + y(2, -1, 1) + z(0, 1 + \iota, 1 - \iota)$ and solve the three equations. Express $x$ and $y$ in terms of $z$ first.
problems.solution:
We must solve \[ \begin{aligned} 2\iota x + 2y &= 1, \\ x - y + (1 + \iota) z &= 0, \\ y + (1 - \iota) z &= 1. \end{aligned} \] From the third equation $y = 1 - (1 - \iota) z$. Substituting in the second, \[ x = y - (1 + \iota) z = 1 - (1 - \iota) z - (1 + \iota) z = 1 - 2z. \]
Now the first equation becomes \[ 2\iota (1 - 2z) + 2\big(1 - (1 - \iota) z\big) = 1 \iff (2 + 2\iota) - (2 + 2\iota) z = 1 \iff z = \frac{1 + 2\iota}{2 + 2\iota}. \] Multiplying numerator and denominator by $2 - 2\iota$, \[ z = \frac{(1 + 2\iota)(2 - 2\iota)}{8} = \frac{6 + 2\iota}{8} = \frac{3 + \iota}{4}. \] Then \[ x = 1 - 2z = 1 - \frac{3 + \iota}{2} = \frac{-1 - \iota}{2}, \qquad y = 1 - \frac{(1 - \iota)(3 + \iota)}{4} = 1 - \frac{4 - 2\iota}{4} = \frac{\iota}{2}. \]
Hence the coordinate matrix of $(1, 0, 1)$ in the given ordered basis is \[ \begin{bmatrix} \frac{-1 - \iota}{2} \\[4pt] \frac{\iota}{2} \\[4pt] \frac{3 + \iota}{4} \end{bmatrix}. \] Check: the second coordinate of $x(2\iota,1,0) + y(2,-1,1) + z(0, 1+\iota, 1-\iota)$ is $\frac{-1-\iota}{2} - \frac{\iota}{2} + \frac{(1+\iota)(3+\iota)}{4} = \frac{-1 - 2\iota}{2} + \frac{2 + 4\iota}{4} = 0$, as required; the other two coordinates are checked in the same way.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - Coordinates of $(a,b,c)$ in the ordered basis $\{(1,0,-1), (1,1,1), (1,0,0)\}$
problems.problem:
Let $\mathcal{B} = \{ \alpha _1, \alpha _2, \alpha _3 \}$ be the ordered basis for $\mathbb{R}^3$ consisting of
    \[
        \alpha _1 = (1, 0, -1), \quad \alpha _2 = (1, 1, 1), \quad \alpha _3 = (1, 0, 0).
    \]
    What are the coordinates of the vector $(a, b, c)$ in the ordered basis $\mathcal{B}$?
problems.hint: • Compute $x \alpha _1 + y \alpha _2 + z \alpha _3$ coordinate by coordinate. The second coordinate gives $y$ immediately.
problems.solution:
We look for $x, y, z$ with \[ x \alpha _1 + y \alpha _2 + z \alpha _3 = (x + y + z,\ y,\ -x + y) = (a, b, c). \] The second coordinate gives $y = b$; the third gives $x = y - c = b - c$; the first gives \[ z = a - x - y = a - (b - c) - b = a - 2b + c. \]
Hence \[ [(a,b,c)]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} b - c \\ b \\ a - 2b + c \end{bmatrix}. \] Check: $(b - c)(1,0,-1) + b(1,1,1) + (a - 2b + c)(1,0,0) = (a,\ b,\ c)$.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - Two bases of a subspace of $\mathbb{C}^3$ and the change of coordinates
problems.problem:
Let $W$ be the subspace of $\mathbb{C}^3$ spanned by $\alpha _1 = (1, 0, \iota)$ and $\alpha _2 = (1 + \iota, 1, -1)$.
  1. Show that $\alpha _1$ and $\alpha _2$ form a basis for $W$.
  2. Show that the vectors $\beta _1 = (1, 1, 0)$ and $\beta _2 = (1, \iota, 1 + \iota)$ are in $W$ and form another basis for $W$.
  3. What are the coordinates of $\alpha _1$ and $\alpha _2$ in the ordered basis $\{ \beta _1, \beta _2 \}$ for $W$?
problems.hint:
• To write $\beta _j = x \alpha _1 + y \alpha _2$, the second coordinate gives $y$ at once.
  • For (c), invert the two relations obtained in (b).
problems.solution:
(a) $\alpha _1$ and $\alpha _2$ span $W$ by definition. They are linearly independent, because neither is a multiple of the other: the second coordinate of $\alpha _1$ is $0$ while that of $\alpha _2$ is $1$, so $\alpha _2 \neq c\, \alpha _1$; and if $\alpha _1 = c\, \alpha _2$, comparing second coordinates gives $c = 0$, so $\alpha _1 = 0$, which is false. Hence $\{ \alpha _1, \alpha _2 \}$ is a basis and $\dim W = 2$.
(b) Write $\beta _1 = x \alpha _1 + y \alpha _2 = (x + (1 + \iota) y,\ y,\ \iota x - y)$. The second coordinate gives $y = 1$, the first gives $x = 1 - (1 + \iota) = -\iota$, and then the third coordinate is $\iota(-\iota) - 1 = 0$, as required. So \[ \beta _1 = -\iota\, \alpha _1 + \alpha _2 \in W. \] Similarly, for $\beta _2$: $y = \iota$, $x = 1 - (1 + \iota)\iota = 2 - \iota$, and the third coordinate is $\iota(2 - \iota) - \iota = 1 + \iota$, as required. So \[ \beta _2 = (2 - \iota)\, \alpha _1 + \iota\, \alpha _2 \in W. \] $\beta _1$ and $\beta _2$ are linearly independent: if $\beta _2 = c\, \beta _1$, the first coordinates give $c = 1$ and the second then give $\iota = 1$, impossible (and $\beta _1 \neq c \beta _2$ similarly). Two linearly independent vectors in the $2$-dimensional space $W$ form a basis.
(c) From $\beta _1 = -\iota \alpha _1 + \alpha _2$ we get $\alpha _2 = \beta _1 + \iota \alpha _1$. Substituting into the expression for $\beta _2$, \[ \beta _2 = (2 - \iota) \alpha _1 + \iota (\beta _1 + \iota \alpha _1) = (1 - \iota) \alpha _1 + \iota \beta _1, \] so \[ \alpha _1 = \frac{\beta _2 - \iota \beta _1}{1 - \iota} = \frac{(1 + \iota)(\beta _2 - \iota \beta _1)}{2} = \frac{1 - \iota}{2}\, \beta _1 + \frac{1 + \iota}{2}\, \beta _2. \] Then \[ \alpha _2 = \beta _1 + \iota \alpha _1 = \beta _1 + \frac{1 + \iota}{2}\, \beta _1 + \frac{-1 + \iota}{2}\, \beta _2 = \frac{3 + \iota}{2}\, \beta _1 + \frac{-1 + \iota}{2}\, \beta _2. \] So the coordinates are \[ [\alpha _1] = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1 - \iota}{2} \\[4pt] \frac{1 + \iota}{2} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad [\alpha _2] = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{3 + \iota}{2} \\[4pt] \frac{-1 + \iota}{2} \end{bmatrix}. \] Check: $\frac{1-\iota}{2}(1,1,0) + \frac{1+\iota}{2}(1, \iota, 1 + \iota) = \left(1,\ \frac{1 - \iota + \iota - 1}{2},\ \frac{(1+\iota)^2}{2}\right) = (1, 0, \iota) = \alpha _1$.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - Two perpendicular unit vectors form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$
problems.problem:
Let $\alpha = (x_1, x_2)$ and $\beta = (y_1, y_2)$ be vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that
    \[
        x_1 y_1 + x_2 y_2 = 0, \qquad x_1^2 + x_2^2 = y_1^2 + y_2^2 = 1.
    \]
    Prove that $\mathcal{B} = \{ \alpha, \beta \}$ is a basis for $\mathbb{R}^2$. Find the coordinates of the vector $(a, b)$ in the ordered basis $\mathcal{B} = \{ \alpha, \beta \}$. (The conditions on $\alpha$ and $\beta$ say, geometrically, that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are perpendicular and each has length $1$.)
problems.hint: • For $u = (u_1, u_2)$ and $v = (v_1, v_2)$ write $u \cdot v = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2$. The hypotheses say $\alpha \cdot \alpha = \beta \cdot \beta = 1$ and $\alpha \cdot \beta = 0$. "Dot" a linear relation with $\alpha$ and with $\beta$.
problems.solution:
For $u = (u_1, u_2)$ and $v = (v_1, v_2)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ put $u \cdot v = u_1 v_1 + u_2 v_2$. This is linear in each variable, and the hypotheses read $\alpha \cdot \alpha = \beta \cdot \beta = 1$, $\alpha \cdot \beta = 0$.
Linear independence. Suppose $c\, \alpha + d\, \beta = 0$. Taking the dot product with $\alpha$ gives $c\, (\alpha \cdot \alpha) + d\, (\beta \cdot \alpha) = c = 0$, and taking it with $\beta$ gives $d = 0$. So $\alpha, \beta$ are linearly independent. Since $\dim \mathbb{R}^2 = 2$, two independent vectors form a basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
Coordinates. Let $(a, b) = c\, \alpha + d\, \beta$. Taking the dot product with $\alpha$ and with $\beta$ as above, \[ c = (a, b) \cdot \alpha = a x_1 + b x_2, \qquad d = (a, b) \cdot \beta = a y_1 + b y_2. \] Hence \[ [(a, b)]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} a x_1 + b x_2 \\ a y_1 + b y_2 \end{bmatrix}. \] For example, with $\alpha = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ and $\beta = \left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ the vector $(a,b)$ has coordinates $\left(\frac{a + b}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{b - a}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$.

problems.title: Hoffman and Kunze - $1, e^{\iota x}, e^{-\iota x}$ are independent; change of basis to $1, \cos x, \sin x$
problems.problem:
Let $V$ be the vector space over the complex numbers of all functions from $\mathbb{R}$ into $\mathbb{C}$, i.e., the space of all complex-valued functions on the real line. Let $f_1(x) = 1$, $f_2(x) = e^{\iota x}$, $f_3(x) = e^{-\iota x}$.
  1. Prove that $f_1$, $f_2$ and $f_3$ are linearly independent.
  2. Let $g_1(x) = 1$, $g_2(x) = \cos x$, $g_3(x) = \sin x$. Find an invertible $3 \times 3$ matrix $P$ such that \[ g_j = \sum_{i=1}^{3} P_{ij} f_i, \qquad j = 1, 2, 3. \]
problems.hint:
• For (a), evaluate a linear relation at a few convenient points, such as $x = 0$, $\pi$, $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
  • For (b), use $\cos x = \frac{e^{\iota x} + e^{-\iota x}}{2}$ and $\sin x = \frac{e^{\iota x} - e^{-\iota x}}{2\iota}$.
problems.solution:
(a) Suppose $c_1 + c_2 e^{\iota x} + c_3 e^{-\iota x} = 0$ for all real $x$. Evaluating at $x = 0$, $x = \pi$ and $x = \frac{\pi}{2}$ gives \[ c_1 + c_2 + c_3 = 0, \qquad c_1 - c_2 - c_3 = 0, \qquad c_1 + \iota c_2 - \iota c_3 = 0. \] Adding the first two equations gives $c_1 = 0$, and then $c_2 + c_3 = 0$ and $\iota (c_2 - c_3) = 0$, so $c_2 = c_3 = 0$. Hence $f_1, f_2, f_3$ are linearly independent.
(b) By Euler's formula, \[ g_1 = f_1, \qquad g_2 = \tfrac{1}{2} f_2 + \tfrac{1}{2} f_3, \qquad g_3 = \tfrac{1}{2\iota} f_2 - \tfrac{1}{2\iota} f_3 = -\tfrac{\iota}{2} f_2 + \tfrac{\iota}{2} f_3. \] The coefficients of $g_j$ form the $j$-th column of $P$, so \[ P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{\iota}{2} \\[4pt] 0 & \frac{1}{2} & \frac{\iota}{2} \end{bmatrix}. \]
$P$ is invertible, since \[ \det P = 1 \cdot \left( \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\iota}{2} - \left(-\frac{\iota}{2}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{2} \right) = \frac{\iota}{2} \neq 0. \] In particular, since $f_1, f_2, f_3$ are independent and $P$ is invertible, $g_1, g_2, g_3$ are also linearly independent and span the same subspace of $V$.
